slot.title: Matched grip and the full stroke
slot.lessonGoal: Hold the sticks in matched grip and play a relaxed full stroke that rebounds to its starting height.
objectives: Hold a drumstick in matched grip, with the fulcrum between the thumb and the index finger
Describe a full stroke: the stick starts high, strikes the head, and rebounds to its starting height
Explain why letting the stick rebound keeps the hands relaxed

visuals.intent: A hand holding a drumstick in matched grip, seen so the fulcrum between the thumb and the index finger is plain, for the Learner to copy.
The four moments of a full stroke in order, raised, striking, rebounding, and back at the starting height, so the Learner sees the stick come back up on its own.

lesson.title: Matched grip and the full stroke
lesson.lessonGoal: Hold the sticks in matched grip and play a relaxed full stroke that rebounds to its starting height.
objectives: Hold a drumstick in matched grip, with the fulcrum between the thumb and the index finger
Describe a full stroke: the stick starts high, strikes the head, and rebounds to its starting height
Explain why letting the stick rebound is part of a relaxed stroke

blocks.text: Imagine holding a drumstick above a drum, ready for one hit. For your drum-kit playing, the aim here is a loose hold and a smooth motion down to the drum and back up [1].

The fulcrum is the turning point between your thumb and index finger [2]. At the fulcrum, your thumb lies along the stick, opposite the first knuckle of your index finger [3]. Matched grip means holding the sticks the same way in both hands. Your other fingers wrap loosely around each stick without squeezing [3].

sections.heading: Down to the drum and back

blocks.text: A full stroke is a hit that starts with the stick raised and returns it to its starting height [3]. Your wrist lifts the stick above the drum [3]. You send the stick down to strike, then let it bounce naturally back up [1]. The full stroke has no stopping point between the downward and upward movement [1].

The drum supplies energy for the bounce, so you let that energy help the stick return rather than blocking it [2]. Your thumb and index finger stay in contact with the stick while your fingers and wrists remain relaxed [1]. A relaxed full stroke travels smoothly down to the drum and back to its starting height [1][3].

blocks.caption: The Course’s own illustration shows the stick raised, striking, bouncing back, and returned.
blocks.alt: Four panels labeled Raised, Striking, Bouncing back, and Returned show the same stick above a drum. The tip begins high, moves down to touch the drum, bounces upward, and returns to its original height and angle.

descriptor.caption: The Course’s own illustration shows the stick raised, striking, bouncing back, and returned.
descriptor.alt: Four panels labeled Raised, Striking, Bouncing back, and Returned show the same stick above a drum. The tip begins high, moves down to touch the drum, bounces upward, and returns to its original height and angle.

glossary.definition: The point where a drumstick is supported and can turn.
A way of holding drumsticks with the same hand position on both sides.
A drum hit that begins with the stick raised and ends with it back at the same height.
